method: URLs marked actually consulted were opened and read at the stated locator or as explicitly limited abstracts/index extracts. No abstract, snippet, TOC, or commentary is represented as a full book/article reading.

sources.type: primary ecclesiastical history / document quoted in translation
sources.title: Evagrius Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History III.13–14
sources.exactLocator: Book III, chapters 13–14; Henotikon document begins III.14
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened and read III.13–14 and document text. The salutation explicitly addresses bishops, clergy, monks and laity in Alexandria, Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis; document invokes Nicaea, Constantinople, and Ephesus, and avoids a direct Chalcedonian two-natures formula. Read Walford translation, not Greek critical edition.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Evagrius writes late sixth century, retrospectively, and embeds the document in a pro-Chalcedonian ecclesiastical narrative. The document itself as quoted is not dated 482; standard dating comes from chronology beyond this text. The candidate URL is a tertiary Catholic Encyclopedia entry, not the quoted primary text.
sources.supports: Zeno's regional reconciliation document and its stated addressees/content as transmitted by Evagrius.
sources.doesNotSupport: A universal empire-wide edict; achieved consensus; a direct personal letter from Zeno to a private recipient; exact 482 date solely from the quoted document.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: The action concerns Alexandrian/Egyptian reception of an imperial document, even though the selection map is Constantinople. It is a plausible off-map correspondence issue or later report, not a local publication scene unless framed as a separate Constantinopolitan dispatch. Avoid modern labels for later church bodies.
episodes.recommendation: Retain the caveat that intended audience was regional, not universal. A correspondence mechanic is plausible as fictional play, but do not invent authentic letter wording or imply unity succeeded.

episodes.event: Justinian elevated as co-emperor in April 527; sole rule after Justin I's death in August

sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Marcellinus wrote in Constantinople in the early sixth century, in a court-linked environment; chronicle entry is succinct. The cited entry supports co-rule date, not by itself the date of Justin's death or the exact political transition on 1 August.
sources.supports: Co-emperorship/successor designation on 1 April 527.
sources.doesNotSupport: A coronation or sole rule beginning in April; sole-rule transition date without separate death chronology.

episodes.event: Nika revolt, January 532; fires damage Hagia Sophia and central Constantinople

sources.title: Procopius, Persian Wars I.24
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened and read passage: officials kill rioters; faction members free prisoners; citizens flee across to the opposite mainland; fires destroy the sanctuary of Sophia, Baths of Zeuxippus, palace precinct, colonnades and houses; 'Nika' is the watchword. Target passage only, not entire book.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Procopius is close to the event but writes rhetorically, assigning blame and depicting the rioters as disorderly. Do not use his speeches as verbatim transcript or his totals without corroboration. Correct URL is Wars/1F; candidate War/1A points to a different passage/book segment.
sources.supports: A serious urban insurrection, flight across the strait, fires including the church of Sophia, and threat to imperial control.
sources.doesNotSupport: A precise January day from this excerpt; every neighborhood burning; individualized civilian stories; a fully neutral account of causes or responsibility.

sources.title: Procopius, Buildings I.1.20–25
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read passage: Procopius links the Nika rising to fire at Sophia and Justinian's subsequent rebuilding, names Anthemius and Isidore as architects. Does not date dedication in this passage.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Buildings is an imperial encomium/panegyric, praising Justinian and attributing providential meaning; compare the Wars account. Candidate Fordham page itself was not opened during this audit.
sources.supports: Reconstruction after the fire and named architects in Procopius's account.
sources.doesNotSupport: A neutral account of revolt or a 537 dedication date from I.1 itself.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: The text uses the literary name Byzantium for Constantinople. It states citizens fled to the 'opposite mainland'; do not turn this into a documented mass evacuation route or precise safe quarter. Fire footprint can be broad around central landmarks; no exact modern footprint reconstruction is established here.
episodes.recommendation: Strongly supported as a bounded urban crisis. Attribute political framing to Procopius; separate the 532 damage from rebuilding and dedication in 537.

episodes.event: Rebuilding of Hagia Sophia after 532 fire; dedication in 537

sources.title: Procopius, Buildings I.1
sources.exactLocator: I.1.20–27; architects at I.1.24
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened and read lines covering the destruction, rebuilding, imperial sponsorship, named architects Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, and description of the structure. It says work began 'not long afterwards'; this particular text does not supply the 537 dedication date.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Panegyric and imperial praise; it foregrounds Justinian and does not describe construction labor or financing neutrally. Dedication date needs a chronicle/source independent of this building panegyric.
sources.supports: Reconstruction after the prior Sophia burned during Nika; Justinian's patronage; two named architects; broad architectural description.
sources.doesNotSupport: The detailed construction schedule, labor force, procurement routes, exact building logistics, or the dedication date from this locator.

sources.doesNotSupport: No exact date claim in this audit.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: The actual building site is the enduring Hagia Sophia precinct, but present structure and later modifications should not be projected wholesale into the 532–537 phase. Avoid treating the extant building as an untouched 537 structure or placing fictional resource depots at exact unverified archaeological loci.
episodes.recommendation: Reconstruction is grounded. Keep 'dedicated 537' pending direct chronicle check; present the finite construction task as fictional logistics around documented rebuilding, not a documentary account of supply methods.

episodes.event: Khosrow I captures and sacks Antioch-on-the-Orontes in 540; population deportation and fire in Procopius's account

sources.title: Procopius, Persian Wars II.5–10
sources.exactLocator: Book II, chapters 8–9, especially II.8.14 onward and II.9 on deportees / 'Antioch of Chosroes'
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Search result and page text expose the capture narrative, order to enslave survivors and plunder property, burning/destruction, and later deportation/resettlement account. Relevant chapter was located, but detailed continuous reading of all II.8–10 paragraphs was not completed; treat coverage as partial.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Procopius wrote close to the 540 invasion but has literary/dramatic aims. His numbers of captives/dead and exact dialogue require independent corroboration; avoid repeating figures as census data. His Wars and Buildings differ in tone.
sources.supports: A Persian capture/sack and mass displacement as narrated by Procopius; Khosrow's deportation of Antiochenes to a new settlement is part of the narrative.
sources.doesNotSupport: Verified casualty counts, every civilian's fate, a precise extraction route, or a neutral/complete account of the assault.

episodes.event: Plague reaches Constantinople in spring 542; food/supply crisis and distribution premise need separate evidence

sources.type: primary source with academic critical translation and commentary
sources.title: Procopius, Wars II.22–23, Harvard Science of the Human Past selected translations
sources.exactLocator: Procopius biography/source discussion and Wars II.22–23 translation; especially 2.22.9 for his presence/date
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened institutional Harvard page and read the source introduction/comments and initial text. It says Procopius was present in Constantinople when plague arrived in spring 542, describes himself as eyewitness, and cites critical Greek edition; it notes literary modeling on Thucydides and that Procopius depicts imperial response. Partial source translation/commentary read, not all II.22–23.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Procopius's epidemiological account is literary and cannot establish modern pathogen identity by itself; critical commentary notes literary emulation and a narrative of state response. His account gives no specific empty-granary fact in the read locator.
sources.supports: Plague outbreak reached Constantinople in spring 542, with Procopius an eyewitness; a broad emergency/care setting is historically grounded.
sources.doesNotSupport: An empty granary, a discrete food shortage specifically caused by plague in Constantinople, exact mortality numbers, or a historically documented player-directed distribution policy.

episodes.event: Second Council of Constantinople, 553, condemns the Three Chapters

sources.type: primary council sentence in translated edition
sources.title: Acts/Sentence of the Second Council of Constantinople (553)
sources.exactLocator: Final sentence/anathema section on the Three Chapters
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened council page and read the final condemnation text. It names Theodore of Mopsuestia and writings of Theodoret and the letter attributed to Ibas, including their defenders; it is not a complete reading of the acts/sessions.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Translated conciliar material in an older edition, not a critical edition. The dispute's acceptance was regionally uneven and had major western resistance; the final sentence is one party's official normative statement, not evidence of immediate consensus.
sources.supports: The council's explicit condemnation of the Three Chapters and associated defenders/writings.
sources.doesNotSupport: A simple neutral textual collation operation, unanimous Christian acceptance, or claim that it merely reviewed records without political/theological stakes.

sources.title: Richard Price, The Acts of the Council of Constantinople of 553: With Related Texts on the Three Chapters Controversy
sources.exactLocator: Accessible publication summary and description of early sessions/reception
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read the book page summary only, not the full two-volume edition. Summary says Pope Vigilius and supporters were in Constantinople but absented themselves from first sessions; sessions examined the Three Chapters.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Abstract/book record only. It must not be cited as if Price's full translation/commentary was consulted.
sources.supports: A critical-edition lead and council/pope participation caveat at summary level.
sources.doesNotSupport: Detailed source comparison or account of regional reception beyond the summary.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Council convened in Constantinople, but no exact venue/map footprint established in the directly read final sentence. The council met without Pope Vigilius in attendance despite his presence in the city; avoid implying universal institutional consensus. 'Record comparison' is a gameplay abstraction.
episodes.recommendation: Keep the event as a contested documentary/theological proceeding; design can center comparing texts only as fictional player work and should not imply the council was a neutral archive commission. Cite Price's full critical edition in a complete dossier.

episodes.event: Jerusalem/Aelia capitulates to Arab forces; exact date and Umar meeting narratives uncertain

sources.type: primary contemporary sermon in modern scholarly edition lead

sources.doesNotSupport: A contemporaneous surrender document, exact chronology or verbatim conversation with Umar, or proof that all details are contemporary.

It explains that James Howard-Johnston rejects a multi-year siege, while Marek Jankowiak reconstructs major attack(s) earlier, c. 667–669, and that Theophanes' chronology is problematic. It links bibliography; underlying full books/articles not read in this pass.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Useful explainer by a military historian, but secondary web article is not final scholarly authority. It oversimplifies disagreement in places; cite Howard-Johnston and Jankowiak directly in the dossier.
sources.supports: Do not confidently claim a continuous four-year blockade under 674–678; operations and chronology are actively contested.
sources.doesNotSupport: A final settled alternative date or exact campaign narrative without reading cited scholarship and source traditions.
